articles.title: Scientists went looking for giant trees in Taiwan and found a lost world
articles.summary: Taiwan’s steep, remote mountains have sheltered extraordinary forests containing hundreds of giant Taiwania firs. After years of difficult expeditions, LiDAR mapping, and citizen-science detective work, researchers discovered an 84.1-meter (276-foot) tree, the tallest known in East Asia. They also found dense “temples of giants” where dozens of enormous trees grow together. These ancient forests rank among the world’s most carbon-rich ecosystems.
articles.content:
Taiwan, once widely known as Formosa, conceals a remarkable natural world within its steep and rugged interior. It is one of the few places on Earth capable of supporting truly giant trees, including specimens that rise more than 80 meters above the forest floor.

Since 2014, our group, the 'Taiwan tree seekers,' has worked to find, measure, and document these extraordinary trees. The team brings together professional tree climbers, ecologists, geologists, and remote sensing specialists.

That long search reached a major milestone in 2023, when we identified an 84.1-meter-tall (276-foot-tall) Taiwania fir (Taiwania cryptomerioides). It is now recognized as the tallest tree in Taiwan and all of East Asia. The Indigenous Rukai people have a poetic name for these immense firs: 'The tree that hits the moon'.

Taiwan's Mountainous Landscape

Taiwan's geography helps explain why trees of this size can grow there. The island covers roughly 36,000 square kilometers, making it similar in area to Switzerland. Much of the landscape is mountainous, with 258 peaks rising above 3,000 meters. The highest, Mt. Jade, reaches 3,952 meters.

This wide range in elevation supports an exceptional variety of plant life. An estimated 5,000 plant species grow across Taiwan, occupying environments that extend from humid tropical rainforests near sea level to cold alpine tundra at the highest elevations.

About 60% of Taiwan is still covered by forest, with an estimated 950 million trees growing across the island. Industrial logging from 1912 to 1991 removed much of the original primary forest. However, the steepest and most inaccessible terrain acted as a natural barrier, protecting important areas of old-growth forest that logging crews could not easily reach.

The First Expeditions

Our organized search began in August 2014, when researchers from the Taiwan Forestry Research Institute (TFRI) entered the Cilan conservation area for a major expedition. The goal was to investigate a famous group of giant Taiwania firs known as the 'Chilan Three Sisters'.

Local communities had known about the three trees for many years, but the giants had never been carefully measured or scientifically documented. Our survey showed that the tallest stood 69.3 meters high and had a trunk nearly three meters wide.

The trees drew international attention in 2017, when professional climbers from 'The Tree Projects' in Australia came to Taiwan to photograph the Three Sisters in full. Their work helped introduce the remarkable scale of Taiwan's forests to a wider global audience.

A Difficult Search Near Great Ghost Lake

Encouraged by the discovery, we turned our attention to a more isolated area near Mt. Benya. Reports suggested that the region might contain Taiwan's largest concentration of Taiwania firs. It lies close to Great Ghost Lake, a place considered sacred by Indigenous peoples.

Reaching the area required four days of demanding hiking while carrying heavy equipment. The expedition also revealed a major problem with searching for giant trees from the ground. In an old-growth forest with a dense, multi-layered canopy, visual estimates can be highly misleading.

During that trip, we climbed a tree measuring 71.7 meters. Even so, it became clear that traditional ground surveys alone would not be enough. We needed a more reliable way to examine vast areas of remote forest.

Using LiDAR to Map Giant Trees

Searching among 950 million trees scattered across mountains and deep valleys was like looking for a needle in a haystack. To make the process more efficient, we partnered with remote sensing specialists at National Cheng Kung University and began using LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging).

LiDAR is an advanced 3D scanning method that sends laser pulses from an aircraft toward the landscape below. By recording how long each pulse takes to return, the system can build a detailed 3D model of the terrain and estimate the height of individual trees.

Citizen Scientists Join the Search

Taiwan's steep and irregular terrain created another challenge. Automated software often reported trees as being much taller than they really were, especially when they stood beside cliffs or sharp changes in elevation.

People were better than the algorithm at recognizing these geological 'tricks'. In 2020, the project expanded into a large community effort. Hundreds of Taiwanese citizens began examining LiDAR profile images and helping the researchers eliminate tens of thousands of false candidates.

The scale of the problem was substantial. The automated system had incorrectly measured 93% of the trees it identified. Without citizen scientists reviewing the data, researchers could have spent years traveling to trees that were far shorter than the maps suggested.

By the end of 2022, the collaboration produced the 'Taiwan Giant Tree Map,' which documented 941 individual trees taller than 65 meters.

Finding the 'Heaven Sword'

In January 2023, during the Lunar New Year holiday, we used the new map to investigate the strongest candidate for the title of 'tallest tree'. Reaching it required tracing a river for 20 kilometers, followed by two days of steep uphill hiking.

After climbers reached the crown, they lowered a measuring tape from the highest point to the ground. The final measurement was 84.1 meters.

The tree was named the 'Heaven Sword of the Da'an River,' and it was officially recognized as the tallest known tree in both Taiwan and East Asia.

By early 2026, our continued surveys had identified and climbed ten Taiwania trees taller than 70 meters. Two of them exceeded 80 meters.

Hidden 'Temples of Giants'

The Giant Tree Map also guided us toward exceptional concentrations of massive trees that we call 'temples of giants'. Near Mt. Benya, one hectare of forest contained 11 trees, each more than 65 meters tall.

Ten years after our first journey to the Great Ghost Lake region, we returned and encountered an even more astonishing sight. Roughly 30 giant Taiwania firs were growing together in a dense and ancient 'pure forest'. The scale of the cluster left the team speechless.

Giant Forests as Carbon Vaults

These forests are important not only because of their beauty and size. They may also play a major role in storing carbon and supporting the health of the planet.

In 2024, we joined 15 citizen scientists to conduct a detailed study of the 'Tao Tree' valley, home to Taiwan's third-tallest tree. The goal was to determine how much carbon dioxide the forest removes from the atmosphere and stores in its wood.

The findings were remarkable. The forest's total carbon density (even without counting the massive root systems) reached 1,384.5 Mg/ha.

That figure places Taiwan's giant forests among the most carbon-dense ecosystems in the world, comparable to some of Earth's most celebrated old-growth forests. The 'trees that hit the moon' are more than towering natural monuments. They are also essential guardians of the environment.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery of ancient, giant Taiwania firs in Taiwan's remote forests, including the tallest tree in East Asia. This discovery highlights the ecological importance of these forests as some of the world's most carbon-dense ecosystems, contributing to climate change mitigation. The story involves advanced technology (LiDAR), citizen science, and conservation, with broad environmental significance and detailed context.

articles.title: India connects 124 million rural homes to tap water
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Six years ago, fewer than one in six rural homes in India had a tap water connection. As of mid-July, more than four in five do, and the difference adds up to 124 million additional households. Minister V. Somanna confirmed the numbers in a written reply to India’s Rajya […]
The post India connects 124 million rural homes to tap water first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Six years ago, fewer than one in six rural homes in India had a tap water connection. As of mid-July, more than four in five do, and the difference adds up to 124 million additional households.

Minister V. Somanna confirmed the numbers in a written reply to India’s Rajya Sabha: 156.7 million of the country’s 193.6 million rural households now have tap water as of July 16. When the Jal Jeevan Mission launched in August 2019 (its full name, “Har Ghar Jal,” means water for every home), only 32.3 million rural households, about 16.7 percent, had it. It has run as a partnership between the central government and the states.

How the mission scaled

Getting there required regular government reviews with states, field teams sent to slower-moving regions, and money. When costs rose during the COVID-19 pandemic and the supply disruptions that followed, the guidelines were revised in June 2022 to make more central funding available.

What the assessments found

Connection numbers only go so far. A 2022 independent assessment found 86 percent of connected households had working taps, and of those, 85 percent were getting adequate water, 80 percent on a regular schedule, and 87 percent at quality standards. The pipes are working. The 2024 assessment is underway. Data by district and village is publicly available.

articles.personality_title: India brings tap water to 124 million rural homes in six years
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Six years ago, only a small number of rural homes in India had tap water. At that time, fewer than one in six households in villages could turn on a tap for clean water.

**What happened** – By July 2024, more than four out of five rural homes in India now have tap water connections. This means 124 million more homes gained access since 2019, when the government started the Jal Jeevan Mission, also called "Har Ghar Jal," which means "water for every home." The program is a partnership between India’s central government and state governments.

**Impact** – This is one of the largest improvements in rural water access anywhere in the world. Having tap water at home helps families stay healthy by providing clean water for drinking, cooking, and washing. An independent check in 2022 showed most taps worked well, supplied enough water regularly, and met quality standards. This progress improves daily life for millions and supports better hygiene and health.

**What’s next step** – The government is continuing to check how well the taps work and how much water households receive. A new assessment is happening in 2024 to track progress and fix any problems. Data about water access is also shared publicly to keep the program transparent.

**One-sentence takeaway** – India’s Jal Jeevan Mission has connected 124 million rural homes to safe tap water, greatly improving life for millions in just six years.

articles.title: Ancient Arctic carbon is pouring into the sea, but the seabed captures most of it
articles.summary: Thawing Arctic permafrost is releasing ancient carbon into the ocean, raising fears that microbes could turn it into greenhouse gases and accelerate climate change. But sediment cores collected near Canada’s Herschel Island reveal a more reassuring twist: most of this land-based carbon becomes buried in the seafloor, while only about 10 percent is converted into gases.
articles.content:
The Arctic's frozen ground contains enormous stores of organic carbon. As permafrost thaws and coastlines erode, some of that carbon is carried into the ocean. There, microorganisms can break it down and release greenhouse gases that contribute to climate change.

Until now, scientists have had limited information about how much of this carbon returns to the atmosphere and how much remains trapped in the ocean. Researchers from the Alfred Wegener Institute and MARUM - Centre for Marine Environmental Sciences at the University of Bremen have now examined this process along the permafrost coast of Qikiqtaruk (Herschel Island) in Canada.

By studying sediment cores, the team found that large amounts of carbon from land are preserved in the seafloor. They also discovered that marine microorganisms behave like selective eaters, favoring fresh carbon from the ocean over older carbon released from permafrost. The findings were published in Nature Geoscience.

Vast Carbon Stores Are Beginning to Thaw

Permafrost ecosystems on Arctic land contain about 1,300 gigatonnes of organic carbon, much of it from plant remains. Another 400 gigatonnes are stored in ocean sediments and river deltas.

As the planet warms, the Arctic is heating faster than any other region. This rapid temperature rise is causing frozen ground to thaw and coastlines to break apart. Carbon that was previously locked in the soil can then reach the Arctic Ocean through rivers and coastal erosion.

"Consequently, up to 0.02 gigatonnes are entering the sea each year, and according to forecasts, this outflow could rise by 70 to 150 percent by the year 2100," says Dr. Manuel Ruben, lead author of the study from the Alfred Wegener Institute, Helmholtz Centre for Polar and Marine Research (AWI). "However, how much of this is released back into the atmosphere as a greenhouse gas and how much is stored in the seabed has, until now, been largely unknown."

Resolving that uncertainty is important because scientists need to know where the carbon ultimately ends up to estimate how thawing permafrost could affect the climate.

Sediment Cores Reveal Where the Carbon Goes

To investigate, the researchers collected sediment cores from several locations off the coast of Herschel Island. These cores contain layers of material deposited over roughly 50 years.

The results showed that only a relatively small share of the carbon swept into the ocean becomes part of the active carbon cycle.

"Although the sea here carries away huge quantities of organic carbon from the coast, surprisingly little of it ends up in the ocean's active carbon cycle," says Manuel Ruben. "Microorganisms convert around ten percent of the organic carbon from the sediments into gases, which rise into the water and can then enter our atmosphere."

Most of the remaining carbon stays buried in the seabed.

Chemical Clues Track Microbial Activity

The scientists analyzed the composition of the sediment cores and measured how quickly material from the permafrost accumulated on the ocean floor.

They also studied dissolved inorganic carbon found in tiny spaces between sediment particles, known as pore water. These measurements reveal how much CO2 microorganisms have released after consuming organic material.

The isotopic makeup of the pore water helped the team determine where that material came from.

"Carbon isotopes represent our atomic indicators that can identify the food source of the microorganisms," says Prof. Gesine Mollenhauer, a geochemist at the AWI and co-spokesperson for the 'The Ocean Floor - Earth's Unexplored Interface' cluster of Excellence. "The 13C isotope, for example, tells us whether they have consumed carbon from land or from the sea. By way of the 14C isotope, we were able to determine whether the single-celled organisms preferred old organic carbon from permafrost or fresh organic carbon from algae remains."

"Gourmet" Bacteria Prefer Fresh Carbon

The results suggest that the organisms living in the sediment are not equally interested in every type of carbon.

"The sediment is home to 'gourmet' bacteria that apparently prefer fresh carbon stemming from, for example, more recent algal remains over the 'old' carbon from permafrost deposits," explains Gesine Mollenhauer.

Because the microbes favor fresh marine material, older carbon from thawing permafrost may contribute less to atmospheric greenhouse gas levels than scientists once feared.

However, the researchers caution that the full picture is not yet clear.

"However, we do need further research here. This is because some of the organic carbon from the permafrost may already have been broken down before it reaches the seabed."

Coastal Carbon Could Reshape Arctic Ecosystems

The movement of carbon from land into the ocean may affect more than greenhouse gas emissions. It can also change the chemistry and biology of coastal waters that support food resources for local communities.

Sediment released by coastal erosion can reduce the amount of sunlight entering the water. Freshly eroded fragments make the coastal ocean cloudy, while dissolved organic carbon can darken the water.

That loss of light can affect single-celled organisms such as algae, which need sunlight to produce biomass and oxygen. This primary production supports a wider food web that includes fish, crustaceans and seals.

The researchers plan to explore these connections further during the international 'Arctic Pulse' campaign scheduled for 2027. Scientists will carry out coordinated observations from the Polarstern research icebreaker, aboard AWI research aircraft and at sites on land. Their goal is to understand how rapid environmental change is transforming Arctic ecosystems.

Improving Arctic Climate Models

"Our study shows, more precisely than ever before, how much carbon is safely stored in the seabed - and just how much of the decomposed material actually originates from the old permafrost," says Manuel Ruben. "This provides an important foundation for climate models that can predict the consequences of permafrost thawing for the global climate."
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery that most ancient carbon released from thawing Arctic permafrost is being safely buried in the seabed rather than converted into greenhouse gases, which mitigates fears of accelerated climate change. This finding has broad implications for climate modeling and understanding carbon cycles, providing hopeful insight into Arctic ecosystem resilience and climate change impact.
articles.personality_title: Ancient Arctic carbon mostly trapped in seabed, limiting greenhouse gas release
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context**
The Arctic has large amounts of frozen soil called permafrost, which holds a huge amount of organic carbon. As the Arctic warms and the permafrost thaws, some of this carbon washes into the ocean. Scientists worried that tiny microbes might turn this carbon into gases that warm the planet.

**What happened**
Researchers from German institutes studied sediment samples near Canada’s Herschel Island. They found that most ancient carbon from the thawing land does not turn into greenhouse gases. Instead, about 90% of it gets buried safely in the ocean floor. Microbes prefer to eat fresher carbon from the ocean, leaving most of the old carbon untouched.

**Impact**
This discovery is important because it shows that less ancient carbon is released into the atmosphere than previously feared. It means the seabed acts like a natural storage, slowing down potential climate change effects. It also helps scientists improve climate models by giving clearer information on where the carbon ends up.

**What's next step**
Scientists plan to continue studying Arctic coastal areas through the 'Arctic Pulse' campaign starting in 2027. They want to learn more about how carbon moves and how it affects Arctic ecosystems, including local wildlife and communities.

**One-sentence takeaway**
Most ancient carbon released by thawing Arctic permafrost is captured in the seabed, reducing its impact on climate change.
articles.personality_title_fr: La majeure partie du carbone ancien de l'Arctique est piégée dans les fonds marins, limitant les gaz à effet de serre
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte**
L'Arctique contient de grandes quantités de sol gelé appelé pergélisol, qui renferme beaucoup de carbone organique. Avec le réchauffement, ce pergélisol dégèle et une partie de ce carbone se retrouve dans l'océan. Les scientifiques craignaient que des microbes transforment ce carbone en gaz réchauffant la planète.

**Ce qui s'est passé**
Des chercheurs allemands ont étudié des sédiments près de l'île Herschel au Canada. Ils ont découvert que la plupart du carbone ancien provenant des terres dégagées ne se transforme pas en gaz à effet de serre. Environ 90 % est enfoui dans le fond marin. Les microbes préfèrent consommer du carbone plus frais venant de l'océan, laissant intact la majorité du carbone ancien.

**Impact**
Cette découverte est importante car elle montre que moins de carbone ancien est libéré dans l'atmosphère que ce que l'on craignait. Le fond marin agit donc comme un stockage naturel, ralentissant les effets possibles sur le climat. Cela aide aussi à améliorer les modèles climatiques en précisant où se retrouve le carbone.

**Prochaine étape**
Les scientifiques prévoient de poursuivre leurs études dans l'Arctique avec la campagne « Arctic Pulse » à partir de 2027. Ils souhaitent mieux comprendre le déplacement du carbone et son effet sur les écosystèmes arctiques, y compris la faune et les communautés locales.

**En une phrase**
La majorité du carbone ancien libéré par le dégel du pergélisol arctique est capturée dans les fonds marins, limitant son impact sur le changement climatique.

articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto**
El Ártico tiene grandes cantidades de suelo congelado llamado permafrost, que guarda mucho carbono orgánico. Con el calentamiento, el permafrost se derrite y parte de ese carbono llega al océano. Los científicos temían que microbios convirtieran ese carbono en gases que calientan el planeta.

**Qué pasó**
Investigadores alemanes estudiaron muestras de sedimentos cerca de la isla Herschel en Canadá. Descubrieron que la mayoría del carbono antiguo que llega del terreno no se convierte en gases de efecto invernadero. Cerca del 90% queda enterrado en el fondo marino. Los microbios prefieren consumir carbono más fresco del océano, dejando intacto la mayor parte del carbono antiguo.

**Impacto**
Este hallazgo es importante porque muestra que menos carbono antiguo se libera a la atmósfera de lo que se temía. El fondo marino actúa como un depósito natural, ralentizando los posibles efectos en el clima. También ayuda a mejorar los modelos climáticos al dar información más clara sobre dónde termina el carbono.

**Próximo paso**
Los científicos planean seguir estudiando las costas árticas con la campaña 'Arctic Pulse' que comienza en 2027. Quieren entender mejor cómo se mueve el carbono y cómo afecta a los ecosistemas del Ártico, incluyendo la vida silvestre y las comunidades locales.

**Una frase clave**
La mayor parte del carbono antiguo liberado por el deshielo del permafrost ártico queda atrapado en el fondo marino, reduciendo su impacto en el cambio climático.

articles.title: The biodegradable, self-cleaning fabric made from living caterpillar fungus
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The sustainable fashion industry has spent years trying to reduce harm: less water, fewer synthetic chemicals, more recycled material. A research team at the Shenzhen Institutes of Advanced Technology went in a different direction. They grew the fabric from a living organism. The material comes from Cordyceps militaris, a […]
The post The biodegradable, self-cleaning fabric made from living caterpillar fungus first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

The sustainable fashion industry has spent years trying to reduce harm: less water, fewer synthetic chemicals, more recycled material. A research team at the Shenzhen Institutes of Advanced Technology went in a different direction. They grew the fabric from a living organism.

The material comes from Cordyceps militaris, a fungus used in traditional Chinese medicine that naturally forms hyphae, fine threadlike filaments that weave into dense networks. Researchers cultivated it into small pellets, pressed those into flexible sheets, and added glycerol to make them pliable.

The resulting fabric can clean itself, and if it tears, placing fresh fungal pellets on the damaged spot causes new fibers to grow back. “A living textile does not mean that the dress is constantly growing during normal use,” Li Ke, the paper’s first author, said. Under dry conditions with little to feed on, the biological activity stops.

What else it can do

The fungal matrix can host other microorganisms. The team demonstrated this by adding an engineered yeast that clings to fungal cell walls to introduce color, and incorporating hyphae from Aspergillus niger, a melanin-rich fungus, for UV protection. They describe the structure as a “plug-and-play platform,” meaning different organisms can be layered in to give the material different properties without changing its base form.

Environmental testing found it degraded fully within 41 days. The team made a prototype dress, but Li was direct about where things stand: this is not replacing cotton anytime soon. The near-term uses he describes are temporary: short-run fashion, exhibition pieces, art installations, biodegradable packaging. “The broader concept could extend beyond clothing wherever a biodegradable structure with locally programmable biological functions is useful,” he said.

The cost structure is a real hurdle. The culture medium accounts for more than 95 percent of production expenses, and getting to commercial scale means finding cheaper nutrient sources and improving the fermentation process, before real-world testing for washability and durability.

The longer aim is to cut down on outside inputs, having the fungus produce its own pigments and functional molecules rather than relying on added organisms. “In the longer term, synthetic gene circuits may enable biological functions to be activated only at selected locations, times or environmental conditions,” Li said.

articles.personality_title: Scientists create biodegradable, self-cleaning fabric from living caterpillar fungus
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The fashion industry often uses a lot of water and chemicals, which can harm the environment. Researchers have been looking for new materials that are better for the planet.

**What happened** – A team at the Shenzhen Institutes of Advanced Technology made fabric from a living fungus called Cordyceps militaris. This fungus grows tiny threads that can be pressed into flexible sheets. The fabric can clean itself and even repair tears by growing new fibers when fresh fungus pellets are added.

**Impact** – This fabric breaks down completely in about 41 days, making it much better for the environment than many traditional textiles. It can also include other tiny organisms to add colors or protect against UV rays. Although it won’t replace cotton soon, it can be used for short-term fashion, art, or biodegradable packaging.

**What's next step** – Researchers want to lower production costs by finding cheaper nutrients and improving how the fungus grows. They also hope to make the fungus produce its own colors and useful molecules, controlled by special genetic tools, for even more advanced features.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Scientists have developed a new self-cleaning, biodegradable fabric grown from living fungus that could offer eco-friendly uses in fashion and packaging.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des scientifiques créent un tissu biodégradable et autonettoyant à partir d’un champignon vivant
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – L’industrie de la mode utilise souvent beaucoup d’eau et de produits chimiques, ce qui nuit à l’environnement. Des chercheurs cherchent de nouveaux matériaux plus respectueux de la planète.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Une équipe des Instituts de technologie avancée de Shenzhen a fabriqué un tissu à partir d’un champignon vivant appelé Cordyceps militaris. Ce champignon produit de petits filaments qui peuvent être pressés en feuilles flexibles. Le tissu peut se nettoyer tout seul et même réparer les déchirures en faisant pousser de nouvelles fibres quand on ajoute des pellets de champignon frais.

**Impact** – Ce tissu se décompose complètement en environ 41 jours, ce qui est bien mieux pour l’environnement que beaucoup de textiles classiques. Il peut aussi accueillir d’autres micro-organismes pour ajouter des couleurs ou protéger contre les rayons UV. Même s’il ne remplacera pas le coton bientôt, il peut servir pour la mode temporaire, l’art ou des emballages biodégradables.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs veulent réduire les coûts de production en trouvant des nutriments moins chers et en améliorant la croissance du champignon. Ils espèrent aussi que le champignon produira lui-même ses couleurs et molécules utiles, contrôlées par des outils génétiques spéciaux.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Des scientifiques ont développé un nouveau tissu biodégradable et autonettoyant à partir d’un champignon vivant, offrant des usages écologiques en mode et emballage.
articles.personality_title_es: Científicos crean tela biodegradable y autolimpiable a partir de un hongo vivo
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La industria de la moda usa mucha agua y químicos, lo que daña el medio ambiente. Los investigadores buscan materiales nuevos que sean mejores para el planeta.

**Qué pasó** – Un equipo del Instituto de Tecnología Avanzada de Shenzhen creó una tela a partir de un hongo vivo llamado Cordyceps militaris. Este hongo produce hilos finos que pueden convertirse en láminas flexibles. La tela se limpia sola y puede reparar rasgaduras si se añaden nuevos pellets de hongo.

**Impacto** – Esta tela se descompone completamente en unos 41 días, lo que es mucho mejor para el ambiente que muchos tejidos tradicionales. También puede incluir otros microorganismos para añadir colores o protección contra rayos UV. Aunque no reemplazará al algodón pronto, puede usarse en moda temporal, arte o empaques biodegradables.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores quieren bajar los costos encontrando nutrientes más baratos y mejorando el proceso de cultivo. También buscan que el hongo produzca sus propios colores y moléculas útiles, controlados con herramientas genéticas especiales.

**Resumen en una frase** – Científicos han desarrollado una nueva tela autolimpiable y biodegradable hecha de un hongo vivo que podría usarse en moda y empaques ecológicos.
